title: Intake and distribution systems
summary: The four distribution layouts and their trade-offs are the most reliable marks here, together with the service reservoir's one-third capacity rule and the duties of the various valves. Hardy Cross network analysis appears in both this subchapter and pipe flow, and the two conditions to state are that flow balances at every junction and head loss balances round every loop. For Nepal, note HDPE's dominance in rural schemes and the reasons for it.

sections.heading: Conveyance and pumping
sections.body:
**Gravity or pumping** is the first decision, and it dominates the whole economics of a scheme:

| | **Gravity** | **Pumping** |
|---|---|---|
| Running cost | **Almost nil** | **Power, fuel, maintenance** |
| Reliability | **Very high** — no moving parts | Depends on power supply |
| Operator skill | Minimal | Trained staff needed |
| Capital cost | May be higher (longer alignment) | Lower if the source is close |
| Requires | **The source above the demand** | — |

**In Nepal's hills a gravity scheme is nearly always chosen where the topography permits**, because the sustainability of a rural scheme depends far more on **running cost and operator skill** than on capital cost. A pumped scheme in a village with unreliable electricity and no trained operator fails within a few years, whatever its design.

**Types of conduit:**

| Conduit | Character |
|---|---|
| **Gravity main** | Flows under gravity from source to reservoir or treatment |
| **Rising main (pumping main)** | Under pressure from pump to reservoir |
| **Pressure tunnel** | Where a hill must be crossed |
| **Canal / aqueduct** | Open channel; cheap but exposed to contamination |

An **open channel must not be used** for treated water, because it is open to contamination — a point questions test.

**Pumps:**

| Type | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Centrifugal** | **The general choice** — high discharge, moderate head, simple, reliable |
| **Multistage centrifugal / turbine** | High head, deep wells |
| **Submersible** | **Tubewells** — motor and pump both in the well |
| Reciprocating (displacement) | Small discharge, very high head |
| **Air lift** | Sandy or corrosive water, deep wells |
| Jet pump | Small domestic installations |
| **Hand pump** | Rural point sources — the commonest pump in the Terai |

**Pump characteristics** and the two relations worth knowing:

> **Power (kW) = ρ g Q H / (1000 η) = 9.81 Q H / η**  with Q in m³/s and H in metres
> **Specific speed N_s = N √Q / H^{3/4}**  (for a pump — note this uses **discharge**, unlike a turbine, which uses **power**)

**NPSH (net positive suction head)** is the concept that governs pump setting:

> **NPSH available must exceed NPSH required**, or **cavitation** occurs

Because NPSH available falls as the **suction lift** increases, a centrifugal pump has a practical suction lift limit of about **6 m** — and less at altitude, where atmospheric pressure is lower. That altitude effect matters in Nepal: a pump that works at Birgunj may cavitate at the same setting in Kathmandu, and certainly higher up.

**Pumps in series and in parallel** — the same distinction as pipes, but inverted in effect:

| Arrangement | Adds | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Series** | **Heads** add; discharge is common | Higher head required |
| **Parallel** | **Discharges** add; head is common | Higher discharge required |

**Duty point** is where the **pump characteristic curve** intersects the **system curve** (static lift plus friction losses). Two consequences follow: as a pipe ages and roughens, the system curve steepens and the **duty point moves to a lower discharge**; and a pump selected for the ultimate demand runs inefficiently in the early years, which is the argument for **multiple smaller pumps** rather than one large one — with a **standby** unit in every case.

sections.heading: Service reservoirs and storage
sections.body:
**Functions of a service reservoir** — four distinct purposes:

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Balancing storage** | Absorbs the difference between the **constant** supply rate and the **variable** hourly demand |
| **Breakdown storage** | Maintains supply during a failure of the source, plant or pumps |
| **Fire reserve** | The high short-duration demand for fire fighting |
| **Pressure** | Provides the head to distribute water at adequate pressure |

**Capacity:**

> **Total capacity ≈ one third of the maximum daily demand** (about 8 hours' supply)

made up of balancing storage (found from a **mass curve**), breakdown storage (typically 25–50% of the daily demand for a critical system), and the fire reserve.

**The mass curve method** for balancing storage: plot **cumulative supply** and **cumulative demand** against time over the day. The **maximum ordinate above** the supply line plus the **maximum ordinate below** it gives the required balancing storage. It is exactly the Rippl method used for reservoir sizing in hydrology, applied over a day instead of a year.

**Types:**

| Type | Use |
|---|---|
| **Elevated (overhead) tank** | Where the ground is flat and head is needed — the familiar water tower |
| **Ground-level (surface) reservoir** | Where a hill provides the elevation — **the normal case in Nepal's hills** |
| Underground reservoir | Where land is scarce or appearance matters |
| Standpipe | A tall cylindrical tank, part of which provides useful storage |

**Where a natural hill exists, a ground-level reservoir on it is far cheaper than an elevated tank** — no structure to build, no seismic vulnerability from a heavy mass on slender columns. That is why Nepali hill schemes almost always use a **reservoir tank sited above the settlement**, and why elevated tanks are a Terai and urban solution.

**Elevated tanks are a seismic liability** and this is worth stating: a large mass concentrated at the top of slender staging is exactly the configuration that performs worst in an earthquake, and several such tanks failed in 2015. The staging must be designed for the full seismic force with the tank both **full and empty** (the empty case can govern for some members), and **IS 1893 Part 2** covers liquid-retaining tanks specifically.

**Water-retaining structures** are designed differently from ordinary RCC: **crack control governs, not strength**. IS 3370 limits the permissible **steel stress** to keep crack widths small — around **115–150 N/mm²** in direct tension, far below 0.87 f_y — so a tank carries considerably more steel than strength alone would require. That is why the working stress method persisted for tanks long after limit state design took over elsewhere, and why a tank designed by strength criteria alone will leak.

sections.heading: Distribution systems
sections.body:
**Methods of distribution:**

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Gravity system** | Reservoir above the town; **no pumping**, most reliable, most economical |
| **Direct pumping** | Pumps feed the mains directly; **pressure varies with demand**, needs continuous pumping and standby |
| **Combined (pumping with storage)** | Pumps fill an elevated reservoir which feeds the mains — **the usual arrangement**, since it combines steady pumping with variable delivery |

**The combined system is normally adopted** because it lets the pumps run at a **constant, efficient rate** while the reservoir handles the hourly variation, and it retains supply through a pump failure.

**The four layouts** — the most examined item in the subchapter:

| Layout | Description | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Dead end (tree)** | A main with branches, each terminating | **Cheapest**; simple to design; fewer valves; easy to lay | **Stagnation** at the ends; **supply cut off** during any repair; only one path to each point |
| **Grid iron (reticulation)** | Interconnected loops; suits a **rectangular street pattern** | **No dead ends**; **water reaches from two directions**; repairs affect a small area; best for **fire fighting** | **Most expensive**; more valves; **complex analysis** (Hardy Cross) |
| **Circular (ring)** | A ring main around a district, with branches inside | Good pressure; suits a well-planned town | Costly; needs more pipe |
| **Radial** | Water pumped from a central tank radially outward, the town divided into zones each with its own tank | **High pressure**; **quick service**; simple hydraulics | Needs **several distribution reservoirs** |

**The dead end system's two defects are worth stating explicitly**, because they are what the other layouts exist to cure:

1. **Stagnation.** Water at the end of a branch is not renewed, so **chlorine residual decays**, sediment accumulates, and bacterial regrowth occurs. Dead ends therefore need **periodic flushing** through a scour valve — an operating cost the layout imposes for ever.
2. **Single path.** Any repair, burst or valve closure cuts off **everything downstream**. In a grid, water arrives from two directions and only a short length loses supply.

**Pressure requirements:**

| Situation | Minimum residual pressure |
|---|---|
| Single storey | **7 m** |
| Two to three storeys | 12 – 17 m |
| **Multi-storey and fire fighting** | **17 – 22 m** and above |
| Maximum desirable | About **70 m** — beyond it, fittings leak and pipes burst |

Excessive pressure is a real problem, not merely a waste: it increases **leakage** (which rises roughly with the square root of pressure), stresses fittings, and causes bursts. In a hilly town the pressure at the bottom of the network can be far above the acceptable maximum, which is why the system is divided into **pressure zones** separated by **break-pressure tanks** or **pressure-reducing valves** — a device essential in Nepal's hill towns and rarely needed in the plains.

**Network analysis — the Hardy Cross method.** Two conditions must be satisfied:

> **ΣQ = 0 at every junction** (continuity)
> **Σh_f = 0 around every loop** (energy)

Assume a flow distribution satisfying continuity at every junction, then correct each loop iteratively:

> **ΔQ = − Σh_f / (n · Σ|h_f/Q|)**

with **n = 1.85 for Hazen–Williams** and **n = 2 for Darcy–Weisbach**. A pipe common to two loops receives **both** corrections. Convergence takes a handful of iterations.

**Hazen–Williams** is the water-supply resistance formula:

> **V = 0.849 C R^{0.63} S^{0.54}**

because its coefficient **C** is tabulated by **pipe material and age** — which is what a designer actually knows, and it accounts for the deterioration of an old main:

| Pipe | C when new | C when old |
|---|---|---|
| **PVC / HDPE** | **150** | 140 |
| Cast iron, cement lined | 130 – 140 | 100 |
| **Cast iron, unlined** | **130** | **80 – 100** |
| Steel | 140 | 100 |
| Concrete | 130 | 120 |

The drop in C with age is substantial — an unlined cast iron main can lose a third of its capacity through **tuberculation** — and it is why a system that worked when built may fail to deliver pressure decades later without any change in demand.

sections.heading: Pipes, fittings and system management
sections.body:
**Pipe materials and their duties:**

| Material | Advantages | Limitations |
|---|---|---|
| **Cast iron (CI)** | Durable, strong, long life | Heavy, brittle, **tuberculates** unless lined |
| **Ductile iron (DI)** | Strong and **ductile**; now the standard for large mains | Cost |
| **Galvanised iron (GI)** | Cheap, easy to join | **Corrodes**; small sizes only |
| **PVC** | **Corrosion-free**, light, smooth, cheap | Brittle in cold, **UV degradation**, low temperature limit |
| **HDPE** | Corrosion-free, light, **flexible**, fusion-jointed | UV degradation, temperature limit |
| **Steel** | Very strong, large diameters, high pressure | Needs corrosion protection inside and out |
| Prestressed concrete (PSC) | Large gravity mains, high pressure | Heavy, needs care in handling |
| Asbestos cement | Historic | No longer used |

**HDPE dominates Nepali rural water supply**, and the reasons are specific to the setting:

| Property | Why it matters in rural Nepal |
|---|---|
| **Light** | Can be **carried by porters** to sites with no road access |
| **Flexible, supplied in coils** | Tolerates **unstable slopes and settlement** without fracturing; fewer joints |
| **Corrosion-free** | No protection needed, long life with aggressive water |
| **Fusion jointed** | Needs a simple heating tool rather than skilled fitters or heavy plant |
| Smooth bore | Low friction loss, so smaller diameters suffice |

Its vulnerabilities are **UV degradation** where laid above ground (so it must be buried or shaded) and **damage by rodents and mechanical impact**.

**Joints:**

| Joint | Used for |
|---|---|
| **Spigot and socket** | CI and DI pipes; caulked with lead or a rubber ring |
| **Flanged** | Pumping stations, valves — **dismantlable** |
| **Expansion** | Where thermal movement must be accommodated |
| **Screwed / threaded** | GI, small diameters |
| **Butt fusion / electrofusion** | **HDPE** |
| Solvent cement | PVC |
| Mechanical / collar | Repairs and connections |

**Valves and appurtenances — the duties table, and each is a standard one-line question:**

| Fitting | Duty | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **Sluice / gate valve** | **Isolation** for repair | At intervals and at junctions |
| **Reflux / non-return (check) valve** | Prevents **backflow** | On a pumping main, downstream of the pump |
| **Air valve** | Releases **accumulated air**, admits air on draining | At **summits (high points)** |
| **Scour (washout) valve** | **Drains and flushes** the main | At **low points** and at dead ends |
| **Pressure relief valve** | Limits surge pressure | On long pumping mains |
| **Pressure reducing valve / break-pressure tank** | Limits pressure in a **low zone** | Where the static head is excessive |
| **Fire hydrant** | Fire fighting | 100–150 m apart in built-up areas |
| **Water meter** | Measurement and billing | At connections and district boundaries |
| Altitude valve | Prevents overflow of a tank | At tank inlets |

**The air/scour pairing is the one to hold: AIR valves at HIGH points, SCOUR valves at LOW points** — because air rises and sediment settles. Accumulated air at a summit reduces the effective pipe area and can stop the flow entirely, which is why a gravity main over undulating ground needs air valves at every crest.

**Leakage and non-revenue water.** Detection methods: **water audit and district metering** (isolating a district and measuring the **minimum night flow**, which is almost entirely leakage), **acoustic listening sticks and correlators**, **step testing**, and **tracer gas**. Control by **pressure management** (the cheapest single measure, since leakage rises with pressure), **active leak detection**, **prompt repair**, and **pipe replacement**.

**District metered areas (DMAs)** are the modern approach: the network is divided into permanently metered zones so that leakage in each can be quantified continuously, rather than being lost in a single citywide figure. It converts an invisible loss into a managed one.

**Intermittent supply** deserves a closing note because it is the norm in Nepali and Indian towns and its consequences are widely misunderstood. When a system is pressurised for only a few hours a day:

- **Contamination is drawn in** through leaks while the main is empty and at negative pressure — so an intermittent supply is a **water quality** problem, not merely an inconvenience;
- **Every household installs a storage tank and often a booster pump**, which is a large private capital cost duplicating what the utility should provide;
- **Demand becomes peakier**, since everyone draws at once during supply hours;
- **Pipes suffer** from repeated filling and emptying, and air entry accelerates corrosion.

Moving from intermittent to **continuous (24×7) supply** therefore improves quality and reduces total system cost even though it appears to increase consumption — a conclusion that runs against intuition and is worth understanding.

formulas.label: Pump power
formulas.expression: P (kW) = 9.81 Q H / η     (Q in m³/s, H in m)
formulas.note: Specific speed for a PUMP uses discharge: N_s = N√Q/H^{3/4}. A turbine's uses power.

formulas.label: Service reservoir capacity
formulas.expression: ≈ one third of the maximum daily demand (about 8 hours' supply)
formulas.note: Balancing storage from a mass curve, plus breakdown storage and fire reserve.

formulas.label: Hazen–Williams
formulas.note: C is tabulated by material and AGE: 150 new HDPE, 130 new CI, falling to 80–100 when tuberculated.

formulas.label: Hardy Cross loop correction
formulas.note: Conditions: ΣQ = 0 at every junction, Σh_f = 0 round every loop. Common pipes get both corrections.

formulas.label: Residual pressure requirements
formulas.expression: single storey 7 m ; multi-storey and fire fighting 17–22 m ; maximum desirable about 70 m
formulas.note: Excess pressure increases leakage and bursts — hence pressure zones and break-pressure tanks in hill towns.

formulas.label: Pumps in series and parallel
formulas.expression: Series: HEADS add.   Parallel: DISCHARGES add.
formulas.note: The duty point is where the pump curve meets the system curve; it shifts as pipes roughen with age.

formulas.label: Water-retaining structure steel stress (IS 3370)
formulas.expression: permissible steel stress ≈ 115–150 N/mm² in direct tension
formulas.note: Crack control governs, not strength — far below 0.87 f_y, so tanks carry much more steel.
